title: Token Build Pipeline — Figma to Platform
content:
nc-001 covers the DTCG format. This covers getting values from Figma into a build, which is where token systems actually fail.

THE CHAIN:
1. SOURCE OF TRUTH. Pick one, in writing. Either Figma variables are canonical and code is generated, or a token repo is canonical and Figma is synced from it. Bidirectional sync is a trap — it produces conflicts nobody can adjudicate.
2. EXPORT. Figma variables out via the Variables REST API, a plugin (Token Studio is the common choice), or `figma_export_tokens` if you are driving the MCP server. Output DTCG-format JSON.
3. TRANSFORM. Style Dictionary is the default tool. It takes DTCG JSON and emits per-platform artefacts: CSS custom properties, SCSS, JS/TS objects, Tailwind config, iOS Swift, Android XML, Compose.
4. CONSUME. Platforms import the generated file. Nothing hand-edits it — a generated file with manual edits is the most expensive kind of drift.
5. VERSION. Tokens ship as a versioned package with a changelog, on the same semver rules as any dependency.

THE DECISIONS THAT DETERMINE WHETHER THIS WORKS:
- MODES BECOME WHAT? Figma modes are a first-class concept; CSS has no equivalent. Decide up front: light/dark as `[data-theme]` attribute selectors, as a media query, or both. Brand modes usually become separate generated files.
- ALIASES SURVIVE OR RESOLVE? Emitting `--text-primary: var(--grey-900)` keeps the chain visible and themeable at runtime. Emitting `--text-primary: #171717` flattens it and loses runtime theming. Keep aliases on the web; flatten for platforms that cannot resolve references.
- NAMING TRANSLATION. Figma's slash hierarchy (`colour/text/primary`) becomes `--colour-text-primary` in CSS, `colourTextPrimary` in JS, `colour_text_primary` in Android. Define the transform once; never let each platform invent its own.
- WHAT IS NOT A TOKEN. Composite text styles, component variants, and layout grids do not round-trip cleanly. Decide what stays Figma-only and document it, rather than discovering it mid-build.

THE FAILURE MODE TO PLAN FOR: the pipeline runs once at kickoff, then someone changes a colour in Figma and does not re-run it. Automate the export on library publish, or accept that the generated files are a snapshot with a date on them.

title: Token and Component Deprecation Lifecycle
content:
Deleting a token breaks consumers. Keeping every token forever produces a system nobody can navigate. Deprecation is the process between those, and most systems do not have one.

THE FOUR STATES, which every token and component should carry:
- EXPERIMENTAL — available, may change without notice, not for production-critical paths.
- STABLE — supported, changes follow semver.
- DEPRECATED — still works, still shipped, but has a named replacement and a removal date. Emits a warning where the platform allows one.
- REMOVED — gone, in a major version, with a migration note in the changelog.

THE DEPRECATION RECORD, per item:
- What replaces it, exactly. `colour/brand/blue-500 → colour/action/primary/default`. A deprecation without a named replacement is just an unanswered question.
- Why it is going. Consolidation, rename, semantic correction, accessibility fix.
- The removal version and date.
- Whether the migration is mechanical (a find-and-replace anyone can run) or requires judgement.

MECHANICS THAT MAKE IT PAINLESS:
- Never repurpose a name. Changing what `colour/primary` points to silently changes every consumer. Deprecate and add.
- Prefix or suffix deprecated items so they sort out of the way in the Figma picker — `zz-deprecated/` is crude and effective.
- Set the variable's description field to the replacement. Figma surfaces it on hover, which is where a designer will actually see it.
- Ship a codemod for mechanical renames. A one-line sed script attached to the changelog moves adoption faster than any amount of documentation.
- Keep a minimum deprecation window — one minor version or one quarter, whichever is longer.

MEASURE IT: count remaining usages of each deprecated token. That number is your migration progress and it is the only honest signal of whether the deprecation landed. If it has not moved in two quarters, the replacement is wrong or the migration is too expensive, and the answer is to fix that rather than extend the window again.

meta.min_window: one minor version or one quarter

title: Token Audit — Coverage, Gaps, and Redundancy
content:
ds-028 is the Figma-side checklist. This is the measurement, which is what turns an audit into an argument you can win.

THE THREE QUESTIONS:
1. COVERAGE — what percentage of visual values resolve to a token? Measure per category, because the aggregate hides the problem. Colour is typically high; spacing middling; z-index, focus, and motion usually near zero.
2. CORRECTNESS — is the right TIER being used? A component referencing a primitive (`grey-900`) instead of a semantic (`text/primary`) is technically tokenised and still wrong, because it cannot be themed. This is the most common finding and it never appears in a simple coverage count.
3. REDUNDANCY — how many tokens hold the same value? Two names for one hex means two intents were conflated, or one is a leftover. Also: tokens with zero usages.

THE PROCESS:
1. INVENTORY. Extract every visual value from both the design files and the code. Figma side: the audit scripts in figma-lore module 09. Code side: grep for hex literals, `px` values outside the token file, and hardcoded easing and duration strings.
2. MAP each value to an existing token, a tier violation, or a gap.
3. CLASSIFY the gaps: needs a new token, should use an existing one, or is a legitimate one-off.
4. QUANTIFY. Count instances, not just distinct values — one hardcoded colour used 200 times matters more than twelve used once each.
5. PRIORITISE by instances × themeability risk. A hardcoded colour blocks dark mode; a hardcoded radius does not.

THE REPORT: adoption percentage per category with a previous-period comparison, the top ten hardcoded values by instance count with their suggested replacements, the tier violations, the redundant and unused tokens, and a migration plan split into mechanical and judgement-required.

MAKE IT NOT RECUR: a lint rule is worth more than an audit. Ban hex literals and raw `px` outside the token file in CI, and the coverage number stops regressing between audits. An audit finds the debt once; the lint rule stops it accruing.

title: Design Debt — What Counts and How It Accrues
content:
Design debt is the gap between the product's current state and the standard it should meet. Naming the categories is what lets you argue for time to fix it.

VISUAL INCONSISTENCY DEBT
- Components in the product that deviate from the system — wrong colour, spacing, or type.
- Multiple treatments for one interaction. Three button styles doing the same job.
- Legacy UI predating the current system and never updated.

STRUCTURAL DEBT
- Patterns designed for an earlier, simpler version of the product that no longer scale.
- Navigation patched with new items until it no longer reflects the information architecture.
- Features added without holistic design, creating isolated islands.
- Layouts that assumed content types the product has since outgrown.

ACCESSIBILITY DEBT
- Known WCAG violations not yet fixed.
- Components that work visually and fail with assistive technology.
- Missing keyboard navigation, focus management, or announcements.

DOCUMENTATION DEBT
- Components in production that are not in the design system.
- Specs that no longer match the implementation.
- Decisions that exist only in one person's head.

IMPLEMENTATION DEBT (the design-relevant part)
- Hardcoded values where tokens exist — this one blocks theming, so it compounds.
- The same component built differently per platform with no documented reason.
- Third-party embeds with their own UI and their own accessibility problems.

HOW IT ACCRUES, in practice: a deadline ships a feature without system components; a growth spurt introduces content types the layout never anticipated; an integration brings its own interface; a nav item is added without an IA review. None of these are mistakes in isolation. Debt is the accumulation, which is why it needs tracking rather than blame.

THE PREVENTION QUESTION worth adding to every design review: does this create design debt, and if so, is that a conscious trade-off with a note attached?

title: Design Debt Audit — Scoring and the Debt Register
content:
THE AUDIT (research, not a fix sprint — keep them separate):
1. SCOPE. Full product, one feature area, or one platform. Unscoped audits do not finish.
2. INVENTORY. Screenshot every screen and state in scope. Catalogue by screen type, component, or flow.
3. CLASSIFY each item: category (dso-004), severity (Critical / Moderate / Minor), frequency (how many instances), and effort (Low / Medium / High — estimated WITH engineering, because designers systematically underestimate implementation cost).
4. QUANTIFY. Instances per issue, estimated user reach, and business risk — compliance, legal, or trust exposure.
5. SCORE: `severity x frequency / effort`. This surfaces the debt causing the most harm per unit of effort, which is the only ordering a roadmap conversation respects.
6. PLAN, in four buckets:
   - QUICK WINS — low effort, high frequency. Token fixes, label corrections, spacing corrections. Do these immediately; they also demonstrate the audit's value.
   - STRUCTURAL PROJECTS — need real design and engineering investment. Schedule into the roadmap; do not pretend they are cleanup.
   - ACCESSIBILITY FIXES — Critical violations first, then a rolling backlog. These have a legal dimension the others do not.
   - WRITE-OFFS — debt in low-traffic areas that a planned redesign will resolve. Document and defer EXPLICITLY. An undocumented deferral returns as a surprise.

THE DEBT REGISTER — the output is a living document, not a one-time report. Per item: description, category, severity, affected screens/components, status (open / in progress / resolved / deferred), owner, target milestone. Review quarterly and re-score, because severity changes as the product changes.

WHY THE REGISTER MATTERS MORE THAN THE AUDIT: a one-off audit produces a document that is stale in a month and ignored in two. A register with a trend line — debt items opened versus closed per quarter — is the artefact that wins dedicated cleanup capacity, because it turns an aesthetic complaint into a tracked metric.

RUN ONE BEFORE ANY MAJOR REDESIGN. It defines the actual scope of the work, and it usually reveals that a third of the "redesign" is unfixed debt that could ship independently and sooner.

title: Component Specification — The Template
content:
do-005 covers handing off a screen. This is the design-system artefact: the spec that lets a component be built once, correctly, without asking.

1. OVERVIEW — name, one-line description, when to use, and WHEN NOT TO USE with the alternative named. The "not" half prevents most misuse.
2. ANATOMY — labelled visual breakdown. Which parts are required, which optional, which repeatable.
3. VARIANTS — size (sm/md/lg), emphasis (primary/secondary/ghost/destructive), layout. Every combination that is legal, and any that are explicitly not.
4. PROPS / API — name, type, default, required, description. Match the Figma component property names to the code prop names; divergence here is a permanent tax.
5. STATES — default, hover, focus, focus-visible, active, disabled, loading, error, selected, read-only. Every state that exists, with its visual treatment. A missing state gets invented downstream.
6. BEHAVIOUR — interaction, keyboard, motion (duration and easing tokens, not descriptions), responsive behaviour, and what happens with content overflow.
7. CONTENT RULES — label length limits, capitalisation, whether the label is a verb, what happens with a long translation, what to do when a value is null.
8. ACCESSIBILITY — role, accessible name source, keyboard interaction map, focus management (especially where focus goes on open and on close), what is announced on state change, and the reduced-motion variant.
9. TOKENS USED — the actual token names per property. This is what makes the spec verifiable: a reviewer can diff the built component against this list.
10. USAGE — do and don't examples with the reason, and related components.
11. CHANGELOG — with status (experimental / stable / deprecated, see dso-002).

THE TWO SECTIONS THAT DO THE MOST WORK: "when not to use" and "tokens used". The first prevents the component being stretched into jobs it was not designed for; the second makes correctness checkable rather than a matter of opinion.

WRITE IT FOR BOTH AUDIENCES. Designers need anatomy, variants, and content rules. Engineers need props, states, tokens, and accessibility. Splitting them into two documents guarantees one goes stale.
